# 4 Maccabees Chapter 1 — The EMET Bible (Literal)
**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Greek MS (Codex Sinaiticus) | **Section:** Philosophical Introduction

---

**1:1** Philosophical most-necessary is the subject I am about to discuss, whether devout-reason is sovereign over the passions — so I counsel you to give earnest heed to philosophy.

**1:2** For the subject is essential to all people, and moreover it brings the highest praise to those philosophically inclined, namely the question whether reason is master of the passions.

**1:3** But it is necessary to decide what reason is and what passion is, how many forms passion takes, and whether reason rules over all of them.

**1:4** Now reason is the mind that with right-counsel chooses the life of wisdom.

**1:5** And wisdom is knowledge of things divine and human and of their causes.

**1:6** This wisdom is acquired through instruction in the law, through which we learn divine matters reverently and human matters to our advantage.

**1:7** The forms of wisdom are prudence, justice, courage, and temperance.

**1:8** Prudence is the most-sovereign of all, for through it reason rules over the passions.

**1:9** Of passions, the two most-comprehensive kinds are pleasure and pain; and each of these is naturally present in the soul as well as the body.

**1:10** With pleasure and pain there are many attendant emotions.

**1:11** Before pleasure stands desire, and after pleasure stands joy.

**1:12** Before pain stands fear, and after pain stands grief.

**1:13** Anger is a passion shared between pleasure and pain, as anyone who reflects carefully will recognize.

**1:14** In pleasure there also exists a malicious-disposition, which is the most manifold of all the passions.

**1:15** In the soul there are arrogance and love-of-money and desire-for-honor and contentiousness and envy and malice.

**1:16** In the body there is greed and gluttony and solitary-pleasure-seeking.

**1:17** Now reason, I suggest, is the guide of the virtues, but over the passions it is sovereign.

**1:18** Observe now first through the things that impede temperance that reason is sovereign over the passions.

**1:19** Temperance consists in mastery over the desires.

**1:20** Of desires, some belong to the soul and some to the body, and reason appears to rule over both kinds.

**1:21** For why is it, when we are drawn toward forbidden foods, that we turn away from the pleasure they would give? Is it not because reason is able to command the appetites?

**1:22** I believe it is. Therefore when we crave seafood and fowl and four-footed animals and all manner of foods forbidden to us by the law, we abstain because of reason's domination.

**1:23** For the passions of the appetites are checked and inhibited by the temperate mind, and all the impulses of the body are bridled by reason.

**1:24** And more than that, reason can even overcome pain through courage.

**1:25** How does this come about? When a person cleaves to his love of wisdom. Even when the body is enfeebled by age or illness or injury, the mind retains its sovereignty.

**1:26** I shall demonstrate this first through the example of Eleazar the priest, then through the seven brothers and their mother.

**1:27** All of these, by despising sufferings even unto death, demonstrated that reason governs the passions.

**1:28** For their virtues I rightly praise these men and that woman who died together; and for their courage and endurance I call them blessed; and because they won victory over passions I esteem them admirable not only to men in general but even to their torturers.

**1:29** And they became the cause of the dissolution of tyranny over their nation, having conquered the tyrant by their endurance, so that through them their fatherland was purified.

**1:30** But I shall now enter at full length upon the discussion, beginning as is my custom by stating my theme, and then I shall proceed to the narrative, giving glory to the all-wise God.

**1:31** The question then is whether reason is sovereign over the passions.

**1:32** We shall determine what reason is, rightly speaking: it is the kind that with wise counsel chooses the life according to wisdom.

**1:33** Wisdom is acquired through instruction in the law, through which we learn divine things reverently and human things to our advantage.

**1:34** The forms of wisdom are prudence, justice, courage, and temperance.

**1:35** The most commanding of these is prudence, by which alone reason rules over the passions.
